historicalPreparationRecord.scope: Visual inspection of manuscript PDF page 6, lines 65–85
findings: The model volume-equivalent diameter is 513 ± 6 km; the principal-axis values 284 × 266 × 224 ± 6 km are explicitly semi-axes, not diameters.

The south-pole flattening, possible ancient basin, approximately 6.2-to-7.8-hour spin change and 6 ± 1 percent excavated-volume interpretation are conditional models; the pole itself is not directly established by this page as observed terrain.

The roughly one-percent equatorial excavation, 60–90-km oblique projectile and 1.7 (+0.2, -0.4) Ga family evolution are simulation interpretations, not directly observed impact history or an independent radiometric age.
The authors distinguish the equatorial-family interpretation from southern-basin simulations that do not explain the present family.

The mass average (2.04 ± 0.03) × 10^20 kg combined with shape-model volume yields bulk density 2.89 ± 0.08 g/cm^3. Earlier Table 4 three-sigma convention remains explicit; this page does not establish local chemistry or porosity.
Ceres and Vesta density/basin comparisons are historical scientific comparisons, not permission to reuse either body’s map.

historicalPreparationRecord.scope: Manuscript PDF pages 7–8, lines 86–110 and references 1–8
findings: Lower water-to-rock fraction and small interior porosity are interpretive assumptions behind the comparison with CM grain density 2.90 ± 0.08 g/cm^3; neither local composition nor measured void fraction follows.
A common starting material with CM-like Ch/Cgh asteroids is a possible scenario. Visible/near-infrared spectral differences and later thermal/impact evolution remain part of that scenario.

Formation at 3–4 Ma after CAIs, failure to reach approximately 820 K silicate dehydration, homogeneous hydrated interior and partial water/silicate separation are conditional thermal-history interpretations, not present temperature, directly observed layers or active plumbing.

The cited bulk albedo 12–17 percent, Ch/Cgh comparison 6 ± 2 percent and approximately 10-percent bright-spot enhancement are author-reported values; this inspection does not calibrate the ESO raster or infer local salt abundance.
The authors explicitly retain bright exogenic material and unresolved fresh-impact ejecta as alternative bright-spot explanations. Salt deposits are not uniquely established.
The page-8 Pallas–Phaethon–Geminid sodium connection is explicitly a hypothesis based on a proposed genealogical association, not direct Pallas sodium detection or confirmed genealogy.
References 1–8 are visually inventoried only; their appearance is not independent full-source verification or licence evidence.
